title: Integrated triboelectric nanogenerator and radiative cooler for all-weather transparent glass surfaces

paper_content.abstract: Sustainable energies from weather are the most ubiquitous and non-depleted resources. However, existing devices exploiting weather-dependent energies are sensitive to weather conditions and geographical locations, making their universal applicability challenging. Herein, we propose an all-weather sustainable glass surface integrating a triboelectric nanogenerator and radiative cooler, which serves as a sustainable device, harvesting energy from raindrops and saving energy on sunny days. By systematically designing transparent, high-performance triboelectric layers, functioning as thermal emitters simultaneously, particularly compatible with radiative cooling components optimized with an evolutionary algorithm, our proposed device achieves optimal performance for all-weather-dependent energies. We generate 248.28 Wm−2 from a single droplet with an energy conversion ratio of 2.5%. Moreover, the inner temperature is cooled down by a maximum of 24.1 °C compared to pristine glass. Notably, as the proposed device is realized to provide high transparency up to 80% in the visible range, we are confident that our proposed device can be applied to versatile applications.
paper_content.introduction:
Sustainable energy scavenged from abundant natural resources is considered to be the foremost and fundamental step towards achieving carbon neutrality and transitioning to an ecologically benign source of power. Among all the clean energy sources associated with climate, e.g., sunlight, raindrops, and wind, are the most ubiquitous and non-depleted in our daily lives. Therefore, previous studies, which have focused on converting natural energy into usable energy, especially electrical energy, e.g., solar cell1–3, piezoelectric4–6, and triboelectric nanogenerators (TENG)7–9, are receiving increasing attention.

Among them, solar cells have garnered spotlight with extensive study owing to their high efficiency10,11. However, solar cells have limitations associated with various weather conditions and pose numerous challenges requiring large areas and high costs. Meanwhile, radiative cooler (RC), an energy saving device that can cool down terrestrial objects without energy input, has gained tremendous attention with an urgent and ever-increasing need to withstand global boiling. Due to the spectral overlap between black body radiation and the atmospheric window (AW, 8–13 μm), the heat from objects can be directly transferred to the cold universe in the form of thermal radiation. By maximizing the emissivity in the AW and the reflectance in the solar spectrum (0.3–2.5 μm), daytime radiative cooling can be achieved even under direct sunlight. While early studies focused on maximizing the cooling effect using photonic structures12–15, more recently, devices considering practical applications are being actively proposed including temperature adaptive16,17, textile18,19, and transparent or colored RC16,20,21. Specifically, transparent RC has significant potential for application as self-cooling systems, by integrating transparent RC into vehicles or buildings for an energy saving strategy that can replace the conventional glass. However, the inherent limitation of RC is the weather-dependency. Because water is highly absorptive, RC becomes inefficient in rainy weather affecting the transparency of the atmosphere. The inconsistency in cooling performances and regional dependency decreases its versatility, hindering integration in real-life scenarios.

Meanwhile, studies on energy conversion beyond solar resources have been actively pursued to address weather-dependent challenges. Globally, approximately two-thirds of the year have clear days, whereas the remaining one-third experiences rainfall22. Traditionally, to harness energy from rain including abundant renewable energy, hydroelectric power plants are adopted23,24. However, these approaches tend to be bulky and involve astronomical infrastructure costs. Recently, a methodology has been proposed to directly convert mechanical energy from liquid–solid contact electrifications and electrostatic induction during the raindrop process25,26. TENG, distinguished by notably high instantaneous power density compared to other energy converting elements such as piezoelectricity and pyroelectricity27,28, emerges as an effective inducible energy source. Moreover, TENG has advantages in terms of being lightweight, cost-effective, highly reliable, and providing a wide range of material choices. With limitless possibilities for advancement, study is being conducted to elucidate the mechanism of raindrop TENG and explore structural developments29,30. In particular, efforts are underway to integrate raindrop TENGs with solar cells to enable functionality even in sunlight conditions31,32. However, no existing study explores the integration of RC into raindrop TENG.

Herein, we propose a hybrid energy harvesting and saving glass surface that integrates TENG and RC (TeRC) for all-weather conditions (Fig. 1a). The proposed TeRC consists of multiple layers designed for various purposes (Fig. 1b). The upper part on the glass substrate consists of layers for triboelectricity generation and electrodes, while the lower part includes layers for reflecting solar spectrum and emitting thermal energy. Moreover, by systematically designing transparent (Fig. 1c), triboelectric layers particularly compatible with radiative cooling components, TeRC can expand horizons of weather-dependent energy while providing versatile self-powered applications, e.g., wireless sensors, Internet of Things, and barren environment monitoring.
paper_content.results:
Design of TENG part in TeRC
To understand the principle by which TeRC generates electricity through raindrops, it is essential to investigate charge carrier, the predominant mechanism of liquid–solid contact electrification (i.e., triboelectrification). According to the hybrid electric double layer (EDL) model26,33,34, during which the first droplet collides with an electrically pristine solid surface, the interatomic potential barrier decreases due to the overlap of the electron cloud when the interatomic distance is within the repulsive region, resulting in electron transfer (Supplementary Fig. 1). The transferred electrons and the chemically absorbed ions on the solid surface form an electrostatic field, resulting in the formation of an electrostatically induced opposite charge of equal magnitude on the lower electrode. When the next droplet collides with an accumulated negatively charged solid surface, the positively charged ions contained within the droplet are attracted to the solid surface due to the electrostatic induction effect, forming an EDL at the liquid–solid interface (Fig. 2a).

A triboelectric layer, an electret material with high charge storage capability, determining TeRC performances must possess a high hydrophobicity which promotes easy droplets sliding, leaving minimal residual droplets. To identify the optimal layer, various transparent polymer films are compared based on contact angle and surface roughness. The contact angle measurement reveals that fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) exhibits the highest contact angle of 111.8° (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 2), which suggests that FEP film is the most hydrophobic, enabling droplets to roll off its surface effortlessly. Additionally, surface roughness for each film is evaluated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 3) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 3). The results definitively demonstrate that FEP film has the most substantial surface roughness among the measured films, which implies that increased roughness plays a crucial role in enhancing surface hydrophobicity, significantly improving triboelectrification. Therefore, throughout this study, we adopt FEP film as the triboelectric layer.

To investigate the behavior of electrons between TeRC and droplets, we represent schematics of the droplet sequence flowing on TeRC (Fig. 2e) and captured corresponding snapshots (Fig. 2f). The proposed TeRC adopts a two-electrode configuration to extract electrical energy by combining electrostatic induction and triboelectrification, transforming interfacial to bulk effect to avoid interfacial screening effect, while also reducing structural complexity26; a thread-like conductive tape is attached as a top electrode, while the lower electrode is composed of an indium tin oxide (ITO) layer sputtered on a glass substrate. The two electrodes are directly connected to the load resistance RL, forming a closed-loop system with the droplet. After the droplet collides with the FEP surface, the triboelectricity generation is categorized into five stages based on the droplet movement: (i) When the droplet contacts with an electron-accumulated FEP surface, the cations in the droplet bind with the electrons on the FEP surface, forming a pseudo capacitor CF at the contact interface. (ii) While the droplet flows along the surface, charge transfer to the external circuit does not occur until it contacts the top electrode, maintaining a switch-off state. (iii) When the droplet contacts the top electrode, new pseudo capacitors are formed between the triboelectric layer and droplet CE1, as well as between the top electrode and droplet CE2. Consequently, a closed-loop is established with the droplet resistance Rdrop, transitioning to a switch-on state. Then, electrons previously stored in CF rapidly flow to the lower electrode (Supplementary Fig. 4). (iv) During droplet shrinkage, electrons return to the top electrode, and CF is recharged by CE1 and CE2. The spreading and shrinking of droplets represent the charging and discharging phenomena of the pseudo capacitors. (v) As the droplet continues to flow away from the top electrode, the electricity generation cycle ends. To measure triboelectric performance of TeRC, we configure the experimental setup to release droplets at the drop height hdrop and the drop angle θdrop (Fig. 2g).

Furthermore, TeRC has a self-cleaning and antifouling ability from outdoor contamination owing to strong hydrophobic surface, which effectively prevents the reduction in triboelectric performance (Fig. 2h). To assess this, chalk powders are employed as dust, and the ink-ed water to facilitate easy identification of residue on the surface. When water is dropped on the conventional glass, it tends to stay, hindering effective cleaning in the presence of dust and leaving residue on the surface. In contrast, when water is dropped on TeRC, droplets easily roll off, carrying away the powder, in this case, TeRC can be effortlessly cleaned with droplets.

TENG performance of TeRC
Throughout this work, we keep RL, film thickness d, hdrop, θdrop, frequency, droplet volume, and water type fixed at 10 MΩ, 250 μm, 45 cm, 45°, 2.5 Hz, 40 μL, and tap water, respectively, to explore the influence of each parameter. In this configuration, we measure the electrical signal of a single droplet in open-circuit conditions (Fig. 3a). When the droplet touches the top electrode, an instantaneous pulse-like electrical signal is measured, reaching up to 415.43 V, and electrons are released from CF. After discharging, a notable observation reveals the detection of a negative signal with the shrinking of droplet, indicating the backflow of electrons attributed to the recharged CF by CE1 and CE2. To calculate the output power, we sweep RL (0.1–10 MΩ), to extract voltage signals (Fig. 3b). By dividing the output power by the maximum spreading area of the droplet Sdrop, we calculate the power density, reaching a maximum value of 248.28 Wm−2 at 0.5 MΩ. Moreover, the transfer charge q also reaches the maximum value of 30.53 nC at the identical RL (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 5). Furthermore, TeRC produces 2.95 μJ of energy from a single droplet at identical RL, serving as an indicator for evaluating harvested energy (Supplementary Fig. 6).

The selection of the triboelectric layer is a crucial factor in determining the triboelectric performance. The voltages are extracted using various polymer films previously employed for the comparison of hydrophobicity (Fig. 3c). The peak voltage of the droplet over 10 s is highest for FEP of 317.57 V, while the output voltage from other films aligned with the hydrophobic tendency. Notably, the electrical signal using polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is not detected after the first droplet, because the prolonged shrinkage time of the droplet leads to the merging of subsequent droplets, resulting in the electrical cancellation effect (Supplementary Fig. 7). Consequently, we verify that higher hydrophobicity generates a more stable and higher triboelectric performance (Supplementary Fig. 8).

If we assumed that FEP film is much thicker than EDL, the voltage loaded CF can be simplified35,36:

V = qd / (ϵFEP Sdrop)

where ϵFEP represent the permittivity of FEP film. The output voltage is proportional to d, and we experimentally confirm that the output voltage increases with d of FEP film (Fig. 3d). Moreover, in terms of RC part of TeRC, a thicker FEP film functions as a thermal emitter with higher absorption capability in the infrared (IR) range (Supplementary Fig. 19).

In addition, we analyze the output voltage according to hdrop, observing an increase in output voltage with hdrop (Fig. 3e). As hdrop increases, the velocity where the droplet impacts the FEP film also increases. Then, with the increasing Weber number, more electrons participate in triboelectrification26,37. Notably, the droplet inherently carries gravitational potential energy, and the energy conversion ratio η is a crucial factor to evaluate the renewable energy source. By comparing the electrical energy derived from the output power, η records a consistent value about 2.5% regardless of hdrop, which confirms that potential energy is stably converted into electrical energy (Supplementary Fig. 9).

Triboelectric performance also depends on θdrop. The peak voltage increases with θdrop, reaching its peak at 45°, and decreases as θdrop becomes larger, because the contact electrification is closely associated with Sdrop and the electricity discharging time38,39 (Fig. 3f). As θdrop increases, due to the droplet skimming the surface, Sdrop decreases, leading to a reduction in the involvement of electrons in electrification. On the other hand, as the discharging time decreases, the time available for the electrification reaction diminishes (Supplementary Fig. 10). Thus, these two variables synthetically influence the triboelectric performance.

TeRC can be applied to various situations beyond raindrops, such as ocean environments. However, previous studies have reported a reduction in triboelectric performance owing to seawater, but the investigation into the underlying causes has been insufficient40,41. To assess this potential, we evaluate the triboelectric performance based on the potential of hydrogen (pH) of droplets (Fig. 3g). We observe an increasing trend in the output voltage as the pH shifted from acidic to alkaline. This may be attributed to the higher concentration of hydron with decreasing pH, inducing a screening effect that hinders electrostatic induction42,43. However, considering that the pH of global seawater is ~8.1, it can be inferred that the poor triboelectric performance of seawater may not be primarily influenced by pH. Therefore, we compare electrical signals by adjusting salinity using sodium-chloride (NaCl), and observed that as the practical salinity unit (psu) increases, the triboelectric performance deteriorates (Fig. 3h). This is because dissolved NaCl dissociates into Na+ and Cl−, and as psu increases, the ion concentration rises. The excessive free ions in the droplet, caused by the high ion concentration, induced a screening effect. Additionally, we evaluate the potential of TeRC system in real environments by verifying its triboelectric performance using rainwater, and confirmed its ability to maintain excellent electricity generation capabilities (Supplementary Fig. 11).

Design of RC part in TeRC
To cool down an enclosed space under direct sunlight while maintaining visible transparency, the following optical properties should be met; (i) High reflectivity in ultraviolet (UV) and near-infrared (NIR) regions, (ii) high transmittance in the visible region, (iii) high emissivity in the AW, and (iv) high thermal radiation absorption of the inner enclosed system (Fig. 4a). To this end, RC is composed a solar reflector with high AW emissivity material and thick polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) layer. The reflector consists of two parts; the dielectric-metal-dielectric (DMD) layer, a thin metal film sandwiched between dielectric layers, and the bottom Bragg mirror (Fig. 4b). The permittivity of the dielectric used in the DMD layer is much greater than that of the metal, restricting the surface plasmon coupling and reducing absorption, making it transparent in desired frequencies and strongly reflecting NIR light44,45. Here, we have chosen titanium dioxide (TiO2) and silver (Ag) for high permittivity contrast. To further improve NIR reflection, we devise an additional Bragg mirror layer at the bottom with alternating silicon dioxide (SiO2) and TiO2 layers. Keeping the thickness of the Ag layer fixed to 24 nm, the rest of the thickness profile of the multilayer structure is optimized to have high transparency in the visible and high reflection in UV and NIR using the particle-swarm-optimization algorithm (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15). Finally, the PDMS layer is placed at the bottom which is responsible for the IR radiation absorption of the system beneath it for effective cooling of an overheated enclosed space46.

The optimized TeRC shows a high visible transparency maximum of 95.7% and an NIR solar reflectance maximum of 88.3% (Fig. 4c). The fabricated TeRC exhibit slightly reduced visible transparency maximum of 80.0%, and NIR solar reflectance maximum of 70.9%, and overall higher absorptance than the optimized structure (Fig. 4d). This discrepancy is attributed to inherent losses in the actual materials including TiO2, Ag, and ITO (Supplementary Fig. 16). Notably, considering that the TENG-only part in TeRC registers a measured visible transmittance below 84.7% (Supplementary Fig. 17), it is expected that the fabricated sample aligns with or falls below this threshold. However, despite the observed discrepancy, the fabricated TeRC maintains commendable level of visible transmittance, enabling clear visibility (Fig. 1c).

Furthermore, the measured emissivity covers all of the AW indicating effective thermal radiation to outer space (Fig. 4e). The angular emissivity of TeRC shows omnidirectional radiation (Fig. 4f). The expected colors and transmitted images are visualized based on the simulated and measured spectra (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 18). The color coordinates are (0.3288, 0.3669) for the simulated and (0.3376, 0.4074) for the measured TeRC, showing a greenish color.

RC performance of TeRC
To characterize the cooling potential of TeRC, the cooling power is calculated based on the IR optical spectrum (Supplementary Note 22). To consider TeRC as an alternative to conventional glasses, we evaluate radiative cooling potential by assuming the structure is placed on an absorbing chamber, mimicking transparent glazing of vehicles or buildings where most of the non-reflected light is absorbed inside. We compare the optical and cooling properties of TeRC with TENG-only sample and a conventional bare glass. The radiated power from the sample Prad, power absorption from the incident atmospheric emission Patm, and the incident solar flux absorbed by the sample Psun are simulated under ambient temperature Tamb = 303 K (Fig. 5a). Since the non-reflected light is all absorbed inside the chamber, we set the emissivity ε = 1 − R where R represents reflectance. There is no significant difference for Prad and Patm because of the identical sample temperature and effectively high AW emissivity for all three structures (Supplementary Fig. 19). The most notable difference comes from Psun. The NIR reflecting layers of TeRC contribute to decreased Psun of 411.54 Wm−2, which is significantly lower than that of TENG-only, and the glass samples which are 710.8 Wm−2 and 827.54 Wm−2, respectively. Consequently, TeRC shows the highest cooling power than the two references at various temperatures. (Fig. 5b). Equilibrium temperatures where the cooling power is zero at various non-radiative heat transfer coefficient hcc are also calculated (Fig. 5c). Due to the difference in solar absorption, the equilibrium temperatures of TeRC are lower than those of TENG-only and the glass samples by more than 20 and 40 °C, respectively.

To demonstrate the cooling effect of TeRC, we conduct an outdoor measurement with a chamber setup resembling a perfectly absorbing inner system (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 21). To compare the cooling effect of TeRC to glass and TENG, two reference boxes and an ambient box without the testing sample are measured simultaneously (Fig. 5e). The amount of AW flux emitted by four comparisons are visualized as thermal-IR images (Fig. 5f). The temperature variations are measured over 3 days at the four points; inner temperature of the absorbing chamber in TeRC box TTeRC and in the two reference boxes Tglass and TTENG, the temperature outside the absorbing chamber in the ambient box Tchamber, and ambient temperature outside the acrylic boxes Tamb (Fig. 5g). Notably, TTeRC < TTENG < Tglass shows the TeRC can cool down inner temperature of an enclosed space under direct sunlight by reflecting undesired energy in the non-visible solar spectrum range. TTeRC < Tglass also attributed to strong solar reflection and the large covering area of TeRC sample. The temperature difference between samples is significantly high during the daytime. Specifically, ΔT1 = Tglass − TTeRC reaches maximum 24.1 °C and average of 8.2 °C, while ΔT2 = TTENG − TTeRC reaches maximum 18.0 °C and average 5.7 °C (Fig. 5h).

Prospective application of TeRC
The triboelectricity generated through TeRC can be applied to versatile low-power devices. First, we charge capacitors using a rectifier diode circuit (Fig. 6a). By charging the capacitor, a stable electrical supply is achieved, and we successfully charge a 1 μF capacitor to 2 V in ~50 s (Fig. 6b). Moreover, we demonstrate the potential of TeRC by powering a hundred light-emitting diodes (LEDs) using raindrop energy (Fig. 6c, Supplementary Fig. 22, and Supplementary Movie 1). Furthermore, to demonstrate the potential real-world applicability of TeRC, we arrange multiple TeRCs in an array and measure their electricity generation, proving that the TeRC array produces electrical energy at a much higher frequency than a single TeRC (Supplementary Fig. 23). In addition, we evaluate the geographical dependency of TeRC using global long-term-mean precipitation in July47 (Fig. 6d). The precipitation is predominantly concentrated near the equator, known for dense tropical rainforests. In these regions, TeRC can be utilized for supplying power to harsh environments.

Subsequently, the global radiative cooling power is estimated. The cooling power highly depends on the sample temperature and the incident solar irradiation, meaning local weather conditions can substantially affect TeRC performance. To evaluate the cooling effect compared to the pristine glass, the cooling flux difference ΔPcool = Pglass − PTeRC is calculated based on the Earth ambient air temperature and solar irradiance in July48. The sample temperature is set equal to the Earth ambient air temperature (Supplementary Fig. 24). The calculated map portrays strong geographical dependency due to regional climate differences (Fig. 6e). Regions with high solar power tend to have higher differences owing to strong reflecting properties of TeRC in the non-visible solar range. ΔPcool shows a similar distribution pattern with the solar irradiance map, meaning that it has higher potential in regions under strong sunlight (Supplementary Fig. 25). Consequently, we have confirmed that TeRC, with its functionality as both TENG and RC, can perform multifunctionality in the same region according to climate conditions. Additionally, we have identified its potential to be more appropriately applied, considering geographical conditions.
paper_content.methods:
Fabrication
To fabricate the RC part of the proposed TeRC system, titanium dioxide (TiO2), silver (Ag), and silicon dioxide (SiO2) layers are deposited on the backside of indium tin oxide (ITO) glass substrates using electron beam evaporation (KVE-ENS4004, KVT). The 10 × 10 × 0.07 cm3 ITO glass exhibit a resistance of 8 Ω sq−1 and an ITO thickness of 150 nm (TMALAB). The thicknesses of the TiO2 layers were 29, 25, 92, and 94 nm for the first, second, third, and fourth layers, respectively. Between the first and second TiO2 layer, a 24-nm thick Ag layer was deposited. The thicknesses of the first and second SiO2 layers were 112 nm and 168 nm, respectively. A 50-μm thick IR absorber was created using a mixture of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) (Sylgard 184A, Dow Corning) and its curing agent (Sylgard 184B, Dow Corning) in a 10:1 weight ratio. The mixture was spin-coated onto the TiO2, Ag, and SiO2 multilayer at 1400 rpm for 60 s, and then cured at 70 °C for 2 h.

To develop the TENG part of the proposed TeRC system, a 250-μm thick fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) film (FEP0250/004, ALPHAFLON) was attached to all edges of the ITO glass substrate using commercial tape. Subsequently, thread-like conductive fabric tape (GYT12-5020, GT-Wave), consisting of nickel and copper, was attached to the FEP film surface as the top electrode (10 × 0.1 cm2). An identical conductive tape was attached to the ITO surface to form two electrodes. For electricity generation, we opted for conventional conductive tape to enhance durability, as the electrostatic induction on ITO rather than the top electrode plays a dominant role. A syringe pump controlled by a flow regulator was installed at the height hdrop to release water droplets at regular intervals, and the TeRC sample was positioned at the angle θdrop.

Simulation
An in-house rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) code was used for the optical simulations. The monthly long-term-mean precipitation was obtained from CMAP precipitation data provided by the NOAA PSL, Boulder, Colorado, USA. The data for the long-term-mean Earth skin temperature and solar irradiance in July were obtained from the NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project funded by the NASA Earth Science/Applied Science Program.

Measurement
To assess the hydrophobicity of the polymer films, the contact angles were measured by using droplet analyzer (SmartDrop, FEMTO-BIOMED). The surface roughness of the polymer films that served as the dielectric layer in the TENG part was measured using SEM (Regulus 8100, Hitachi) and AFM (Park XE7, Park Systems). The AFM images were recorded in non-contact mode and at room temperature, with a scanning speed of 5 Hz. The droplet size and time sequences were captured using a high-speed camera (FASTCAM SA3, Photron). The output electrical signal was measured using an oscilloscope (DSOX1204A, Keysight) equipped with a 1:10 voltage attenuator (GTP-100A-4, GW Instek). To adjust the pH of the droplets, citric acid was used to lower the pH, and sodium hydrogen carbonate was used to increase it. Sodium chloride was dissolved in the water to adjust salinity.

A UV-visible-NIR spectrometer (Solidspec 3700, Shimadzu) equipped with an integrating sphere was used to measure the transmittance and reflectance of the TeRC sample and the references in the solar spectral range from 0.3 μm to 2.5 μm. Spectralon (Certified Spectralon White Diffuse Reflectance Standard, Edmund Optics) was used for comparison. In the IR regime from 2.5 μm to 15 μm, the spectra were measured using Fourier-transform IR spectroscopy (Nicolet IS-50, Thermofisher Scientific). For all the measurements, the absorptivity was calculated by subtracting the sum of the transmittance and reflectance from unity.

The size of the samples was 100 × 100 mm2. For the measurement chamber, a wooden frame chamber that was 120 mm in height and 100 mm × 100 mm in width, with a 300-mm high and 100 × 100-mm wide acrylic plate was used. The samples were carefully fixed onto a polystyrene sample cradle, to minimize heat conduction. The acrylic plate had holes on its side to allow air to flow. The wooden chamber was covered with aluminum tape, to reflect sunlight, and the top of the chamber was covered with a low-density polyethylene film to avoid convection. To prepare an absorbing chamber with dimensions of 45 mm (length), 45 mm (width), and 15 mm (height), the exterior of the chamber was painted with commercial white paint, to achieve high solar reflectance; black commercial paint was painted on the interior to allow all incoming light to be absorbed in the chamber. The samples were covered with absorbing chamber which was located in a wooden chamber. The inner temperature of the absorbing chamber was measured using Copper wire format K-type thermocouples inside the chamber for the cooler and reference boxes. In the ambient box, the inner temperature of the acrylic box was measured using the same type of thermocouple. The measurement point of the ambient temperature was located outside of the chamber, where free air flowed and sunlight was blocked. All temperatures were measured at intervals of 30 s, using a data logger (OM-CP-OCTTEMP-A-2000, OMEGA Engineering). The wind speed, relative humidity, and dew point were measured using a weather station (HD52.3D, Delta OHM). The IR camera was calibrated for an emissivity of 0.95.

Data availability
The data that support the findings of the study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

Code availability
The simulation and optimization code are available from the corresponding author upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors reported a new window design by combining triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) and radiative cooler (RC). Different from conventional energy harvesting window which mainly utilizes photovoltaic material, the application of TENG and energy harvesting from raindrops opens a new venue for energy efficiency window design. Meanwhile, the data provided is rich and comprehensive. Therefore, I recommend publishing this manuscript in Nature Communication after the authors address the following questions.
1. It is suggested to explain the rationale for adding an IR absorption layer at the back side (Interior faced side) of the window. Based on the previous research (Nano Energy 89, 106440 (2021).; Science 374, 1501-1504 (2021). ), the front side of window should have a high AW emissivity to prompt RC, while the back side of window should have a low AW emissivity. Therefore, I suggest that the authors should reconsider the necessity of adding IR absorption layer at the back side of window.
2. In Fig. 5f, the author showed IR images for glass, TENG, TeRC, and ambient and claimed that the IR images represented the surface temperature of the samples. I suggest that the authors should take precautions when measuring surface temperature via IR camera. As the AW emissivity of glass, TENG, and TeRC are different, the amount of IR emitted by these materials may not represent their actual surface temperature. Therefore, the author may wish to change the statement from "surface temperature of four comparisons" to "amount of AW emitted by four comparisons".
3. Based on Fig. 6d and e, the regions with high application potentials for TeRC include North America, Europe, and part of Asia. As these regions may have both cooling demand in summer and heating demand in winter, the authors should comment on fulfilling both cooling and heating demand in these regions.
4. I am curious about the energy harvesting efficiency of TENG in real-life situations. As a supplementary, the author may consider measuring energy harvesting efficiency of TENG on a rainy day. This suggestion is not compulsory. However, I believe that an on-site demonstration may be helpful to better illustrate the advantage of TeRC window.
5. It is understandable that the manuscript was transferred from Nature Sustainability as Fig. 1C, the photo of the sample has a background with the word "Nature Sustainability". However, as this paper is currently in the reviewing process (and may be published) in Nature Communication, the authors should change the background to avoid ambiguity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors proposed windows that achieve sustainable functionalities in all-weather conditions by combining energy harvesting using triboelectric nanogenerators leveraging liquid-solid electrification in rainy conditions, and energy saving using radiative cooling technology for selectively reflecting, transmitting, and absorbing the solar spectrum energy to regulate indoor temperature. The integration of seemingly unrelated engineering disciplines to address energy challenges has the potential to pioneer new research fields, sparking interest not only within the scientific community but also garnering significant attention from social and economic communities. I think this work is quite interesting and timely and may contribute to the related community. So, I raise some issues and would like to provide some advice on the manuscript before considering the process of publication in Nature Communications as follows.
1. In Figures 4c and 4d, the authors present the simulated and measured results of reflectance, transmittance, and absorptance spectra of the designed TeRC. However, while both results show a similar trend, they cannot be considered entirely reasonable. It’s important to sufficiently explain the cause of these differences or demonstrate through further experiment that the simulation results adequately support the experimental findings.
2. In the process of validating the functionality of the TeRC as a triboelectric nanogenerator, the authors utilized a thread-like conductive tape composed of nickel and copper as the top electrode. Was there a specific criterion for selecting the top electrode? Does the performance of the triboelectric nanogenerator vary when using different types of electrodes?
3. The authors designed the TeRC with a dielectric-metal-dielectric (DMD) reflector-Bragg mirror underneath the glass substrate for radiative cooling functionality. Was there a specific reason for arranging the two systems in this order? Would the optical performance remain the same if the other of the two systems were reversed?
4. To effectively utilize the electrical energy harvested from the TeRC in real applications, current is considered a crucial factor. However, the manuscript primarily described the performance of the TeRC in terms of voltage values. It is requested to provide performance metrics regarding the current of the triboelectric nanogenerator.
5. The TeRC sample used for measuring radiative cooling performance appears quite purple in Figure 5e. In my opinion, the color due to reflection spectra might be more visually prominent than transmission. Could you include calculations for the color based on reflectance?
6. In Figure 5h, it is stated that the TeRC can lower the inner temperature up to a maximum of 24.1 degrees compared to conventional glass. However, in Figure 5f, the surface temperature shown does not appear significantly lower for the TeRC compared to other samples. Is there a reason for this discrepancy? Please explain how the cooling effect on the interior is achieved.
7. Please ensure that the explanations are aligned with the time reference set for illustrating the droplet sequence in Figure 2f and Figure 3a. Based on the Figure 2f, the electrical signal is detected at the moment the droplet contacts the electrode at 6.5 ms. However, it seems that Figure 3a employs a different time scale.
8. Please provide the optical refractive index (n) and extinction coefficient (k) values for the materials used in the design of the TeRC.
9. Please check the logo of the journal used to indicate the transparency of the TeRC sample in Figure 1c with the logo corresponding to Nature Communications.
10. The title used in Supplementary Information is different from the main manuscript. Please check it carefully.
11. The following recommendations should be considered for the next submission: There is a lack of mention and references related the broad field of smart windows. It is recommended that references can be added to enrich the content for the readers, especially those with thermal-, strain-, and/or combined stimulus-responsive materials for windows: [1] ACS Energy Lett. 2023, 8, 5, 2300–2307; [2] Mater. Horiz., 2018, 5, 1000-1007; [3] Joule 2019, 3 ,858–871; [4] ACS Energy Lett. 2020, 5, 4, 1159–1166; [5] Adv. Mater. 2015, 27, 2489–2495; [6] Adv Funct Mater 2023, 33, 2305998.
The concept put forward this manuscript is relevant to the sustainable energy, radiative cooling, and triboelectric nanogenerator literature and the results presented are good to aid the future research in this regard. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Review of all-weather sustainable windows for energy harvesting and saving by Geon Lee et. al.
The work by Lee et. al presents a window structure comprising a exterior-facing tribolelectric nanogenerator and an interior facing radiative cooler. The design is novel and on the materials front, the theory and the characterizations are reasonable. However on the applications front, there are some major issues, detailed below, that I would suggest the authors to meaningfully address before I can recommend their work for publication. In particular, it appears that their design is better suited for vehicles than buildings. Specifically:
1. It seems that the authors missed the fact that the TENG itself is a sufficient radiative cooler, and that there is no need for the PDMS reflective cooler in most situations. The authors claim that an emissive surface like PDMS is needed to remove the heat from indoors. This assumes that the indoors are hotter than the window. However, their window has significant solar absorption, which would make it hot. Also buildings that can afford to employ sophisticated systems like theirs are actively cooled to temperatures that can be quite a bit cooler than the outdoor air, and the window. The role of radiative coolers in that case becomes minimizing heat flow from outdoors rather than enabling heat flow from indoors. In that case, having a low-E surface on the interior may be more beneficial than having a radiative cooler.
Where I see their system being useful are cars, whose dark interiors and significant stationary periods under the sun make the interiors suitable for their design. But buildings seem more suited to a case where they have their TENG radiative cooler coupled with an indoor facing low-E surface. The authors are asked to comment on this, and adjust the scope of their paper accordingly.
2. The authors should provide the R, T and E values of their real design (line 244), and not just the simulations, as that is important to validate the performance of their designs.
3. The authors should explain the mechanism of the triboelectricity generation in more detail, especially since this paper will be read by people from various disciplines. For instance, why do the polymer films in Line 103 have a negative charge? Is it true for all polymers? If so, why? How is the charge regenerated so quickly after the water drops leave?
4. The authors are requested to add details about the optical properties of the TENG in the main text, as that is probably more critical for cooling. Would the authors please clarify if the properties account for all components, like the conductive tape, which covers a fraction of the area of their design? Is it solar absorptive?
5. While I do not doubt the functionality of their design, it is unclear if the authors have done the best experiments to show their design’s benefits. For instance, why is there a PE film above their design in Fig. 5? Windows don’t have PE film above them? If the experiments represent car front windows, then they are fine, but if they represent building windows, should they not be vertical? Is it representative to have a setup that absorbs all transmitted sunlight to become very hot (not true for buildings)? How are the indoor temperatures measured – are the thermocouples shaded from the sun?
6. Also, their cooling power modelling seems to be incorrect. For instance, antarctica has a 0 cooling power in Fig. 6, while Greenland has high cooling power. That does not seem right. Also, using the earth skin temperature for calculations is not correct, they should use ambient air temperatures as a reference. There are ample examples of this. I also would like to suggest that to make calculations simpler, the authors could just do the calculations for a few major cities – a global map is not necessary, and in their case, inaccurate.
7. It was not clear to us whether the authors have included a comparison of their TENG, and an outdoor radiative cooler (which would be just the optical part of the TENG), that would help readers understand the benefit of the triboelectric part.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this manuscript, by rationally integrating transparent triboelectric layer and radiative cooler on a glass substrate, the authors demonstrate the combination of triboelectric nanogenerator and radiative cooling in a single window, enabling all-weather energy harvesting and saving. The design is novel and inspirational, but I don’t think the manuscript meet with the high requirement of nature communications.
1. The discrepancy of real RTA from the simulated results, as explained by the authors, arises from inherent losses in FEP and ITO. I wonder how the FEP film was attached onto the ITO side of the glass. If there is an air gap left between them, the optical performance would be deteriorated.
2. The authors did not give demonstration of the durability and real-environment performance of TENG, evaluation of possibility of scaling up the sustainable window, and comparison of energy saving and harvesting amount of RC and TENG part. Prospective applications should be enriched to better support the authors’ outlook.
3. For TENG, peak power density is measured, but total energy output of a single raindrop is not given. As the resistance of the load increases, it is expected that the release of charges takes up a long period, and so the total energy output may increase. It is suggested that the total energy output should be measured for different load resistance. The discussion part gives an unrealistically high value of 0.446 kWh in an hour. This value should be recalculated based upon total energy output instead of upon peak power density to reveal real output capability.
4. At the beginning of Result section. The description on the electrification mechanism of triboelectric layer is confusing. Triboelectrification (or contact electrification) refers to the microscopic separation or generation of positive and negative charges caused by contact or friction, which originates from the overlap of electron wave function of different materials (refer to: 10.1016/j.mattod.2019.05.016), instead of due to electrical discharge as implied in your description. Triboelectrification produces the negative charges on the polymer film, not the opposite. According to literature (10.1038/s41586-020-1985-6), the continuous impinging of droplets generates the negative charges. The electric discharge is occurred at the stage that the droplet contacts the top electrode, which forms the electric signal in external circuit. This is the working mechanism of droplet-based TENG, not the triboelectrification process.
5. You mentioned raindrops carry positive charges before reaching the polymer. That’s true. However, even if the raindrops are strictly electrostatically neutral, they become positively charged after impinging the polymer, during which triboelectrification leads to charge transfer from the droplet to the polymer. This process takes place not due to electrical discharge between raindrop and polymer, but due to microscopic solid-liquid interaction and charge transfer. As raindrops continuously collide, triboelectric negative charges on the polymer accumulate till saturation. As a result, the original positive charges on the raindrops barely contribute to this process. It is safe to conclude that the effect of the positive charges on the raindrops due to colliding with air particles do not contribute to triboelectrification. The triboelectrification process should be rewritten.
6. “the geographical dependency of the two climate conditions exhibits a complementary effect,” the complementary effect of the two climate conditions also seems that the “multifunctional” of TeRC is unnecessary, because there is only one part (TENG or RC) workable in some places.

This hybrid electric double layer (EDL) model consists of a “two-step” process. In the initial
phase, molecules and ions within the liquid collide on the solid surface through thermal
motion and pressure. Consequently, the electron clouds of solid atoms and water molecules
overlap, facilitating electron transfer between them. Notably, materials possessing a high
electron-capturing capability can directly acquire electrons from water molecules, including
ions. This electron transfer involves a transition from high-energy states to low-energy states,
ensuring that if the energy variation of electrons is lower than the potential energy barrier,
the transferred electrons can be retained on the surface. In the second step, the electrified solid
surface attracts free ions in the next droplet through electrostatic interaction, resulting in the
formation of an EDL. This constitutes the mechanism of triboelectrification occurring at the
liquid–solid interface. In our original manuscript, we omitted a detailed explanation of this
process and inadvertently failed to distinguish between triboelectrification and the
mechanism of droplet-based triboelectric nanogenerators, potentially causing confusion for
the reviewer. Therefore, in the revised manuscript and supplementary information, we have
provided detailed explanations of triboelectrification occurring at the liquid–solid interface.
Additionally, we have modified the description of electron behavior in the droplet sequence
of droplet-based triboelectric nanogenerators as follows.
Moreover, we will explain the reason why the polymer film becomes negatively charged, as
raised by the reviewer. When a droplet collides with a virgin solid surface, water molecules
and surface atoms come into close proximity. During this process, electron transfer occurs
due to the overlap of electron clouds in the repulsive force region. Electron transfer occurs
from water molecules to the solid surface. This is because polymers, especially those with a
large number of fluorine groups such as fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) or
perfluoroalkoxy (PFA), possess a strong electron-withdrawing ability, leading to a significant
electron transfer effect during the contact electrification process with liquids. For this reason,
we evaluated the triboelectricity generation capability of various polymers (FEP, PFA,
polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and polyester (PET)) and confirmed that all polymers generate
triboelectricity, but polymers with fluorine groups exhibit outstanding output performance.
Therefore, we have modified statements in the revised manuscript to ensure that readers can
easily understand the basic principles of triboelectricity generation. Additionally, we have
added the following contents to the supplementary information.

Comment 4: At the beginning of Result section. The description on the electrification
mechanism of triboelectric layer is confusing. Triboelectrification (or contact electrification)
refers to the microscopic separation or generation of positive and negative charges caused by
contact or friction, which originates from the overlap of electron wave function of different
materials (refer to: 10.1016/j.mattod.2019.05.016), instead of due to electrical discharge as
implied in your description. Triboelectrification produces the negative charges on the
polymer film, not the opposite. According to literature (10.1038/s41586-020-1985-6), the
continuous impinging of droplets generates the negative charges. The electric discharge is
occurred at the stage that the droplet contacts the top electrode, which forms the electric
signal in external circuit. This is the working mechanism of droplet-based TENG, not the
triboelectrification process.
Response 4: We would like to express our gratitude to the reviewer for providing critical

Additionally, we apologize for any confusion caused to the reviewer regarding the
explanation of the working mechanism of triboelectrification (i.e., contact electrification) in
our proposed TeRC system.
To actively accommodate the reviewer’s comment, we will first explain the
triboelectrification effect occurring in the liquid–solid interface. The mechanism behind
triboelectrification has long been a subject of inquiry, with various hypotheses proposed over
time. In examining the working mechanism of triboelectrification, it is important to pay close
attention to what entity initiates the movement of charge. However, recent research results by
Professor Wang’s group have revealed that both electron transfer and ion adsorption
(chemical interaction) are involved in triboelectrification [R4.4.1-2].
[R4.4.1] Wang, ZL. et al. On the origin of contact-electrification. Mater. Today 30, 34-51
(2019).
[R4.4.2] Lin, S. et al. Contact electrification at the liquid–solid interface. Chem. Rev. 122(5),
5209-5232 (2022).
This hybrid electric double layer (EDL) model consists of a “two-step” process. In the initial
phase, molecules and ions within the liquid collide on the solid surface through thermal
motion and pressure. Consequently, the electron clouds of solid atoms and water molecules
overlap, facilitating electron transfer between them. Notably, materials possessing a high
electron-capturing capability can directly acquire electrons from water molecules, including
ions. This electron transfer involves a transition from high-energy states to low-energy states,
ensuring that if the energy variation of electrons is lower than the potential energy barrier,
the transferred electrons can be retained on the surface. In the second step, the electrified solid
surface attracts free ions in the next droplet through electrostatic interaction, resulting in the
